title: 04 — Algorithms & Problem Patterns
html:
04 — Algorithms & Problem Patterns

Premise: you don't memorise 500 problems. You learn ~15 patterns, recognise which one a problem is wearing, and adapt. This file is the pattern catalogue plus the classical algorithms a senior engineer is expected to know cold.

1. Complexity analysis — the parts people get wrong

1.1 Growth rates

Big-O n=10 n=1,000 n=1,000,000 Typical source
O(1) 1 1 1 Hash lookup, array index
O(log n) 3 10 20 Binary search, balanced tree, heap op
O(n) 10 10³ 10⁶ Single scan
O(n log n) 33 10⁴ 2×10⁷ Comparison sort, divide & conquer
O(n²) 100 10⁶ 10¹² ❌ Nested loops, naive pair comparison
O(2ⁿ) 1024 ∞ ∞ Subsets, naive recursion
O(n!) 3.6M ∞ ∞ Permutations, brute-force TSP

Practical ceiling: ~10⁸ simple operations per second per core. So for a 1-second budget:

  • n ≤ 10⁶ → O(n log n) fine
  • n ≤ 10⁴ → O(n²) fine
  • n ≤ 20 → O(2ⁿ) fine
  • n ≤ 10 → O(n!) fine

This table lets you infer the intended complexity from the constraints — the single most useful interview trick.

1.2 Things the notation hides

  • Constants matter in reality. O(n log n) quicksort beats O(n) radix sort for small n. Two O(n) algorithms can differ 20× on cache behaviour.
  • Amortised ≠ average ≠ worst. Dynamic array append is amortised O(1) (occasional O(n) resize). Hash lookup is average O(1), worst O(n). A latency-sensitive p99 cares about the worst, not the average.
  • Space includes the call stack. Recursive DFS on depth n is O(n) space and can StackOverflowException (uncatchable in .NET — process dies).
  • Output-sensitive complexity: "find all pairs summing to k" is at least O(number of pairs) — you can't beat the output size.
  • Analyse the right n. O(V+E) — is your graph sparse or dense? O(n·m) for two collections — which one dominates?

1.3 How to derive it fast

  1. Count loops and their bounds (nested and dependent: for i; for j=i..n → n²/2 → O(n²)).
  2. Recursion → Master theorem: T(n) = a·T(n/b) + O(n^d)
    • d > log_b a → O(n^d) (work dominated by the split)
    • d = log_b a → O(n^d log n) (merge sort: a=2,b=2,d=1 → O(n log n))
    • d < log_b a → O(n^log_b a) (naive Karatsuba-style)
  3. Data structure operations → look up the cost, multiply by call count.
  4. Amortise anything that only occasionally does big work.

2. Sorting

Algorithm Best Average Worst Space Stable In-place Use when
Insertion O(n) O(n²) O(n²) O(1) ✔ ✔ n < ~20, or nearly sorted. Used inside every real sort
Merge O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n) ✔ ✘ Stability required, linked lists, external sort
Quick O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n²) O(log n) ✘ ✔ General in-memory default; best constants
Heap O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n log n) O(1) ✘ ✔ Guaranteed worst case, no extra memory
Introsort — O(n log n) O(n log n) O(log n) ✘ ✔ What Array.Sort actually is: quick → heap on deep recursion → insertion on small
Timsort O(n) O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n) ✔ ✘ Python's sorted, Java objects — exploits existing runs
Counting O(n+k) O(n+k) O(n+k) O(k) ✔ ✘ Small integer range k
Radix O(d·n) O(d·n) O(d·n) O(n+k) ✔ ✘ Fixed-width keys (ints, dates), large n
Bucket O(n+k) O(n+k) O(n²) O(n) ✔ ✘ Uniformly distributed values

The comparison-sort lower bound is Ω(n log n) — there are n! orderings and each comparison yields 1 bit, so you need ≥ log₂(n!) ≈ n log n comparisons. Radix/counting beat it only by not comparing (they exploit key structure).

Stability matters when you sort by multiple keys sequentially. Sort by name, then stably by department → within each department, names stay ordered. Array.Sort (unstable) breaks that; OrderBy (LINQ, stable) doesn't. ⚠️ Real bug source in report generation.

// LINQ OrderBy is stable; Array.Sort/List.Sort are NOT
var report = rows.OrderBy(r => r.Dept).ThenBy(r => r.Name).ToList();   // explicit is better anyway

External merge sort — the answer to "sort 100 GB with 8 GB RAM":

  1. Read chunks that fit in memory, sort each, write as a sorted run.
  2. K-way merge the runs with a min-heap (O(N log K)). This is exactly what a database does for a SORT operator that spills to tempdb, and what Polars/Spark do for large sorts.

3. Binary search — and the reason everyone gets it wrong

// Classic: find exact index, or ~(insertion point)
static int BinarySearch(int[] a, int target)
{
    int lo = 0, hi = a.Length - 1;
    while (lo <= hi)
    {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;        // NOT (lo+hi)/2 — overflows for large arrays
        if (a[mid] == target) return mid;
        if (a[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1;
        else hi = mid - 1;
    }
    return ~lo;                               // .NET convention: bitwise complement of insert point
}

// The more useful form: leftmost index where predicate becomes true.
// Works for ANY monotonic predicate — this is the version to memorise.
static int LowerBound(int lo, int hi, Func<int, bool> pred)   // [lo, hi)
{
    while (lo < hi)
    {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (pred(mid)) hi = mid; else lo = mid + 1;
    }
    return lo;                                // first index where pred is true
}

Binary search on the answer — the pattern that isn't about arrays at all. If you can check an answer in O(n) and the check is monotonic (if X works, X+1 works), binary search the answer space in O(n log range).

Examples: "minimum ship capacity to deliver in D days", "smallest divisor so the sum ≤ threshold", "minimum time for K workers", "allocate books to minimise max pages", "how many replicas do I need for p99 < 200 ms" (yes, capacity planning is the same shape).

🔍 This is the single highest-value pattern to recognise. If a problem asks to minimise a maximum or maximise a minimum, it's almost certainly binary search on the answer.

4. The pattern catalogue

4.1 Two pointers

Shape: sorted array/string, find a pair/triple, or partition in place. O(n) instead of O(n²).

// Two-sum in a SORTED array
static (int, int)? TwoSum(int[] a, int target)
{
    int l = 0, r = a.Length - 1;
    while (l < r)
    {
        int sum = a[l] + a[r];
        if (sum == target) return (l, r);
        if (sum < target) l++; else r--;      // the invariant: moving in is the only useful direction
    }
    return null;
}

Also: remove duplicates in place, container-with-most-water, 3-sum (sort + fixed outer + two pointers = O(n²)), palindrome check, merge two sorted arrays, Dutch national flag (3-way partition).

4.2 Sliding window

Shape: contiguous subarray/substring with a constraint. Expand right, shrink left while the constraint is violated. Each element enters and leaves once ⇒ O(n).

// Longest substring without repeating characters — O(n) time, O(min(n, charset)) space
static int LongestUnique(string s)
{
    var lastSeen = new Dictionary<char, int>();
    int best = 0, start = 0;
    for (int end = 0; end < s.Length; end++)
    {
        if (lastSeen.TryGetValue(s[end], out int prev) && prev >= start)
            start = prev + 1;                      // shrink past the duplicate
        lastSeen[s[end]] = end;
        best = Math.Max(best, end - start + 1);
    }
    return best;
}

Fixed-size variant: max sum of k consecutive elements — subtract the leaving element, add the entering one. Real-world: rate limiting over a rolling window, moving averages, anomaly detection over a time window, log burst detection.

4.3 Fast & slow pointers (Floyd)

Cycle detection in a list or in a functional graph (nums[i] as an edge — "find the duplicate number" in O(1) space), find the middle, check palindromic list. O(n) time, O(1) space.

4.4 Prefix sums / difference arrays

Precompute cumulative sums → any range sum in O(1) after O(n) build.

var prefix = new long[a.Length + 1];
for (int i = 0; i < a.Length; i++) prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + a[i];
long RangeSum(int l, int r) => prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l];       // inclusive [l, r]

Variants: 2D prefix sums (submatrix sum), difference array for O(1) range updates (add v to [l,r] → diff[l]+=v; diff[r+1]-=v, then prefix-sum once), prefix XOR, prefix product. Combined with a hash map: "count subarrays summing to k" in O(n) — store counts of prefix sums seen, look for prefix - k. Real-world: time-series aggregation, cumulative revenue, histogram bucketing, seat/resource booking over intervals.

4.5 Interval problems

The universal first step: sort by start (or by end for greedy scheduling).

static List<(int S, int E)> Merge(List<(int S, int E)> intervals)
{
    intervals.Sort((a, b) => a.S.CompareTo(b.S));
    var res = new List<(int S, int E)>();
    foreach (var iv in intervals)
    {
        if (res.Count > 0 && iv.S <= res[^1].E)
            res[^1] = (res[^1].S, Math.Max(res[^1].E, iv.E));   // overlap → extend
        else
            res.Add(iv);
    }
    return res;
}
  • Merge intervals — sort by start.
  • Max concurrent meetings / min rooms — sweep line: +1 at each start, −1 at each end, sort events, track running max. Or a min-heap of end times.
  • Non-overlapping max count (activity selection) — greedy by earliest end time. Provably optimal.
  • Insert interval, interval intersection — two pointers over sorted lists.

Real-world: calendar/booking systems, resource allocation, license usage, on-call rotas, Gantt/critical path, network bandwidth reservation.

4.6 Hash map counting / frequency

Anagram grouping, first unique character, top-K frequent (map + heap or bucket sort), subarray sum equals k, LRU (§3 in file 03), two-sum unsorted, detecting duplicates within a window. Rule: whenever a brute-force solution does "for each element, search the rest", a hash map usually collapses it from O(n²) to O(n).

4.7 Backtracking

Shape: build a candidate incrementally, abandon (prune) as soon as it can't lead to a solution.

choose → explore → un-choose

static void Permute(List<int> nums, List<int> current, bool[] used, List<List<int>> output)
{
    if (current.Count == nums.Count) { output.Add([.. current]); return; }
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.Count; i++)
    {
        if (used[i]) continue;
        used[i] = true;  current.Add(nums[i]);
        Permute(nums, current, used, output);
        current.RemoveAt(current.Count - 1);  used[i] = false;   // un-choose
    }
}

Problems: N-Queens, Sudoku, subsets/combinations, word search, palindrome partitioning, expression building, graph colouring. The skill is pruning — without it you're just enumerating. Constraint propagation (Sudoku: track candidate sets per cell) turns intractable into instant. Real-world: SAT/constraint solvers, query planners exploring join orders, dependency resolution (NuGet's resolver), test-case generation, scheduling with hard constraints.

4.8 Divide & conquer

Split → solve independently → combine. Merge sort, quickselect (find k-th smallest in O(n) average — better than sorting), closest pair of points, matrix multiply (Strassen), FFT, binary search, parallel map-reduce. Parallelism note: D&C is the natural shape for Parallel.For, PLINQ, fork/join — independent subproblems.

4.9 Greedy

Take the locally best option; correct only if the problem has the greedy-choice property + optimal substructure. You must justify it — the interview failure mode is applying greedy where DP is needed.

Works greedily Needs DP
Activity selection (earliest end) 0/1 knapsack
Huffman coding Longest increasing subsequence (well, O(n log n) greedy+binary search)
Dijkstra (non-negative weights) Shortest path with negative edges
Fractional knapsack Coin change with arbitrary denominations
Minimum platforms/rooms Edit distance
Coin change with canonical currency (1,2,5,10…) Coin change with (1,3,4) for 6 → greedy gives 4+1+1, optimal is 3+3

Proof techniques: exchange argument ("any optimal solution can be transformed into the greedy one without getting worse") or "greedy stays ahead".

4.10 Dynamic programming

Conditions: optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems. Method — always in this order:

  1. Define the state precisely in words: dp[i][w] = max value using the first i items with capacity w.
  2. Write the recurrence (the decision at each state).
  3. Set base cases.
  4. Choose memoisation (top-down) or tabulation (bottom-up).
  5. Optimise space — usually only the previous row is needed.
// 0/1 knapsack — O(n·W) time, O(W) space after rolling-array optimisation
static int Knapsack(int[] weights, int[] values, int capacity)
{
    var dp = new int[capacity + 1];
    for (int i = 0; i < weights.Length; i++)
        for (int w = capacity; w >= weights[i]; w--)      // reverse: each item used at most once
            dp[w] = Math.Max(dp[w], dp[w - weights[i]] + values[i]);
    return dp[capacity];
}

// Edit distance (Levenshtein) — O(n·m)
static int EditDistance(string a, string b)
{
    var prev = new int[b.Length + 1];
    var cur  = new int[b.Length + 1];
    for (int j = 0; j <= b.Length; j++) prev[j] = j;
    for (int i = 1; i <= a.Length; i++)
    {
        cur[0] = i;
        for (int j = 1; j <= b.Length; j++)
            cur[j] = a[i-1] == b[j-1]
                ? prev[j-1]
                : 1 + Math.Min(prev[j-1], Math.Min(prev[j], cur[j-1]));  // sub, delete, insert
        (prev, cur) = (cur, prev);
    }
    return prev[b.Length];
}

The DP families to recognise:

Family Signature Examples
Linear / 1D dp[i] depends on dp[i-1..i-k] Fibonacci, climbing stairs, house robber, LIS (O(n²) or O(n log n) with patience)
Knapsack Choose/skip with a budget 0/1, unbounded, subset sum, partition equal subset, coin change
Two-sequence dp[i][j] over two strings LCS, edit distance, regex/wildcard matching, sequence alignment (bioinformatics)
Interval dp[i][j] over a range, split at k Matrix chain multiplication, burst balloons, palindrome partitioning, optimal BST
Grid dp[r][c] Unique paths, min path sum, maximal square
Tree DP Post-order over children House robber III, tree diameter, independent set
Bitmask DP State = subset (n ≤ ~20) TSP, assignment problem, "visit all nodes"
Digit DP Count numbers with a property Count of numbers ≤ N with no repeated digits

Real-world DP: diff algorithms (git, Monaco editor use Myers, an LCS variant), spell check/fuzzy search, DNA alignment, resource allocation/portfolio optimisation, query plan cost optimisation, text justification, RL value iteration.

4.11 Graph traversal patterns

Signal in the problem Use
"shortest number of steps", unweighted BFS
"all reachable", "connected components", "islands" DFS or BFS (flood fill)
"shortest path with weights ≥ 0" Dijkstra
"cheapest with at most K stops" Bellman-Ford / BFS with levels
"order respecting dependencies" Topological sort
"detect a cycle" DFS colouring / Kahn's / DSU (undirected)
"connect all with minimum cost" MST (Kruskal/Prim)
"spreading from multiple sources" (rotting oranges, fire spread) Multi-source BFS — seed the queue with all sources
"grid + obstacles + shortest" BFS on the grid as an implicit graph
"bidirectional" BFS from both ends, meet in the middle

4.12 Heap / Top-K

See file 03 §6. Signals: "k largest/smallest/most frequent", "merge k sorted", "median of stream", "schedule by priority", "minimum cost to connect ropes".

4.13 Cyclic sort / index-as-hash

When values are in range [1..n], place each value at its index → find missing/duplicate in O(n) time, O(1) space. Signals: "array contains numbers 1 to n", "find the missing/duplicate number".

4.14 Bit manipulation

| Trick | Meaning | |---|---| | x & (x-1) | Clears the lowest set bit → count bits (Brian Kernighan), power-of-two test (x & (x-1) == 0) | | x & -x | Isolates the lowest set bit (Fenwick trees use this) | | a ^ b ^ b == a | XOR self-inverse → find the single non-duplicate in O(1) space | | 1 << i, mask \| (1<<i), mask & ~(1<<i) | Set membership as bits | | BitOperations.PopCount/LeadingZeroCount | Hardware-accelerated in .NET | Real-world: permission flags ([Flags] enum), bitmaps/bitsets for large sparse membership, compression, hashing, feature flags, colour manipulation.

4.15 Meet in the middle / two-phase

Split an exponential problem into two halves, enumerate each (2^(n/2)) and combine. Turns 2⁴⁰ into 2×2²⁰. Also the shape of MapReduce, bidirectional BFS, and "compute both directions then combine" array problems (product of array except self, trapping rain water).

5. String algorithms

Problem Algorithm Complexity
Substring search KMP (prefix function) / Boyer-Moore (skip) O(n+m) / sublinear average
Multiple pattern search Aho-Corasick (trie + failure links) O(n + total pattern length + matches)
Rolling-hash comparison Rabin-Karp O(n+m) average
Longest palindromic substring Manacher O(n) (expand-around-centre O(n²) is usually fine)
Suffix problems Suffix array + LCP / suffix automaton O(n log n) build
Fuzzy match Levenshtein DP, trigram similarity, BK-tree O(n·m)
Tokenisation/parsing Finite state machine O(n)

Real-world: log parsing, grep, WAF rules, spam filtering, search relevance, diffing, syntax highlighting, virus signature scanning, autocomplete.

⚠️ String performance in .NET: strings are immutable — concatenation in a loop is O(n²). Use StringBuilder, string.Create, String.Join, or Span<char>. Interpolated strings are optimised in modern .NET but not inside loops. For parsing hot paths, ReadOnlySpan<char> + MemoryExtensions methods avoid all allocation.

6. Numerical / practical algorithms worth knowing

Algorithm Use
GCD (Euclid) gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a%b) — fractions, cycle lengths, LCM
Modular exponentiation Cryptography, hashing; O(log e)
Sieve of Eratosthenes All primes ≤ n in O(n log log n)
Reservoir sampling Uniform sample from an unbounded stream
Fisher-Yates shuffle Unbiased shuffle in O(n) — ⚠️ OrderBy(_ => Random) is biased and O(n log n)
Consistent hashing Distribute keys across nodes with minimal reshuffle on membership change — sharding, caches, load balancers
Token bucket / leaky bucket Rate limiting
Exponential backoff with jitter Retry policy that doesn't synchronise clients
HyperLogLog / Count-Min Approximate cardinality/frequency at scale
Bloom filter Membership pre-filter
Merkle tree Efficient diff/verification of large datasets (Git, blockchains, Dynamo anti-entropy)
CRDTs Conflict-free merge for offline-first / collaborative editing
Vector clocks / Lamport timestamps Causality in distributed systems
Raft / Paxos Consensus (see file 08)
Rsync rolling checksum Delta sync of large files 
// Consistent hashing with virtual nodes — the core of cache/shard placement
public sealed class HashRing
{
    private readonly SortedDictionary<uint, string> _ring = new();
    private readonly int _virtualNodes;

    public HashRing(IEnumerable<string> nodes, int virtualNodes = 150)
    {
        _virtualNodes = virtualNodes;
        foreach (var n in nodes) Add(n);
    }

    public void Add(string node)
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < _virtualNodes; i++)
            _ring[Hash($"{node}#{i}")] = node;        // vnodes smooth the distribution
    }

    public void Remove(string node)
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < _virtualNodes; i++)
            _ring.Remove(Hash($"{node}#{i}"));
    }

    public string GetNode(string key)
    {
        if (_ring.Count == 0) throw new InvalidOperationException("Ring is empty");
        uint h = Hash(key);
        foreach (var (pos, node) in _ring)            // first node clockwise
            if (pos >= h) return node;
        return _ring.First().Value;                    // wrap around
    }

    private static uint Hash(string s) =>
        BitConverter.ToUInt32(System.Security.Cryptography.MD5.HashData(
            System.Text.Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(s)), 0);
}

Why it matters: with hash(key) % N, adding one node remaps ~all keys (cache-wide miss storm). With consistent hashing, only ~1/N of keys move. Virtual nodes fix the uneven-distribution problem of plain ring placement. In production, a SortedDictionary scan should be a binary search over a sorted array — shown as a dictionary here for clarity.

7. Recursion: rules that prevent bugs

  1. Base case first, and make sure every path reaches it.
  2. Progress toward the base case on every call (smaller n, fewer items, shorter string).
  3. Trust the recursion — assume the recursive call is correct for smaller inputs, then handle the combine step. (This is the leap most people struggle with.)
  4. Bound the depth. .NET default stack is 1 MB → ~10–50k frames. Deep recursion on user data is a crash vector; convert to an explicit stack.
  5. Memoise if subproblems repeat, otherwise you're doing exponential work.
  6. Tail recursion is NOT optimised by the C# compiler / CLR reliably (unlike F#/functional languages) — don't rely on TCO in C#.
// Recursive → iterative conversion, the general recipe: your own stack
static void IterativeDfs(Node root)
{
    var stack = new Stack<Node>();
    stack.Push(root);
    while (stack.Count > 0)
    {
        var n = stack.Pop();
        Visit(n);
        for (int i = n.Children.Count - 1; i >= 0; i--)   // reverse to preserve order
            stack.Push(n.Children[i]);
    }
}

8. A method for solving an unseen problem (use this in interviews)

flowchart TD
    A[Read the problem] --> B[Restate it in your own words<br/>+ confirm with the interviewer]
    B --> C[Ask about constraints:<br/>n range, value range, duplicates,<br/>sorted?, memory, streaming?]
    C --> D[Work a small example BY HAND<br/>including an edge case]
    D --> E[State the brute force + its complexity<br/>— always have a working answer]
    E --> F{What does the constraint<br/>suggest?}
    F -->|n ≤ 20| G[Bitmask / backtracking]
    F -->|n ≤ 10^3| H[O n² DP acceptable]
    F -->|n ≤ 10^5-10^6| I[O n log n: sort, heap,<br/>binary search, two pointers]
    F -->|n ≥ 10^7 or streaming| J[O n single pass /<br/>approximate structure]
    G --> K[Pick the pattern, state the invariant]
    H --> K
    I --> K
    J --> K
    K --> L[Code it — clear names, no cleverness]
    L --> M[Dry-run on the example + edges:<br/>empty, single, all-same, max, overflow]
    M --> N[State final time/space + one trade-off<br/>you would change in production]

Edge cases to test every time: empty input, single element, all identical, already sorted, reverse sorted, negatives/zero, integer overflow, duplicates, max size, null/None.

9. Where algorithms actually show up in your day job

Business problem Underlying algorithm
Portfolio overlap between funds Set intersection / hash join; if weighted, cosine similarity
Deduplicating client records MinHash + LSH, or DSU over match pairs
Reconciliation between two datasets Sort-merge join, or hash join; diff = LCS
Batch job dependency execution Topological sort
Retry scheduling Priority queue + exponential backoff
Rate limiting an API Token bucket / sliding-window counter
Cache eviction LRU / W-TinyLFU
Sharding customers across DBs Consistent hashing
Which report rows changed Merkle tree / hash comparison
Best route / cheapest allocation Dijkstra / min-cost flow / LP
Search ranking Inverted index + BM25 + top-K heap
Time-series downsampling Reservoir sampling / LTTB
Fuzzy name matching (KYC) Levenshtein + phonetic (Soundex/Metaphone) + trigram index
Fraud ring detection Connected components on a transaction graph
Query optimisation DP over join orders

10. Study plan and checklist

8-week plan (2 problems/day, ~1 hour):

Week Focus
1 Arrays, two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums
2 Hash maps, strings, sorting
3 Stacks/queues, monotonic stack, intervals
4 Binary search (incl. on the answer), heaps/top-K
5 Trees: traversal, BST, recursion patterns
6 Graphs: BFS/DFS, topo sort, Dijkstra, DSU
7 DP: 1D → knapsack → two-sequence → grid
8 Backtracking, bit manipulation, mixed timed sets

Rules that make practice work: 25-minute timer then read the solution; re-solve from scratch 3 days later (spaced repetition is the whole game); keep a one-line note per problem of the pattern, not the code; always state complexity out loud.

Self-check — can you, from memory:

  • Write binary search with no off-by-one, including the lower-bound form
  • Explain why merge sort is O(n log n) via the recursion tree
  • Implement BFS and DFS on a grid and on an adjacency list
  • Implement Dijkstra with a priority queue, and say why it fails on negative edges
  • Write topological sort and use it to detect a cycle
  • Do 0/1 knapsack and edit distance with space optimisation
  • Implement an LRU cache in O(1)
  • Explain consistent hashing and why % N is wrong for caches
  • Derive the complexity of a recursive function with the Master theorem
  • Recognise "minimise the maximum" → binary search on the answer
